# Documentation Standards

Documentation should be discoverable, current, and useful. Documentation that is out of date is often worse than no documentation.

---

## Principles

- Write for the person joining the team tomorrow
- Document the *why*, not just the *what* — code explains what, documentation explains context
- Keep documentation close to the code it describes
- Treat documentation as part of the [Definition of Done](../delivery/definition-of-done.md)

---

## What to Document

| Type | Where |
|------|-------|
| Architecture decisions | [Architecture Decision Records](../operations/architecture-decision-records.md) |
| Service overview | README in the repository |
| Runbooks | [Operational Excellence](../pillars/operational-excellence.md) |
| Data models | dbt docs / data catalogue |
| APIs | OpenAPI / inline docstrings |
| Onboarding | Team wiki or handbook |

---

## What Not to Over-Document

- Avoid documenting what the code already makes obvious
- Don't write comment blocks explaining *what* a function does if the name says it
- Don't maintain documentation that duplicates the code — it will drift

---

## Suggested Tooling

| Tool | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `dbt docs` | Auto-generate data model documentation |
| MkDocs / Docusaurus | Engineering handbooks |
| Confluence / Notion | Team wikis |
| OpenAPI / Swagger | API documentation |

Use whatever fits the team. The tool matters less than the habit.
